items.stem: Test H₀:X~Uniform(0,1) against H₁:X~N(0,1), at level α with 0<α<1. Which statements are correct?
statements: A most powerful test exists for every α in (0,1).
A most powerful test fails to exist for some α in (0,1).
items.explanation: The Neyman–Pearson lemma gives a most powerful test. Under H₀ the support is (0,1), but under H₁ the normal density is positive on the whole real line. Thus the test must reject outside (0,1), where rejection costs no size. Within (0,1), the likelihood ratio φ(x) decreases for x>0, so the remaining size α is assigned to 0<x≤α. The full region is (−∞,0]∪(0,α]∪[1,∞), up to boundary conventions. The two regions printed in C and D omit the alternative-only support, so only A is true as written.

A.why: The Neyman–Pearson likelihood-ratio ordering supplies an MP test for every prescribed size.

B.why: A most powerful test exists for each 0<α<1.

C.why: The displayed set omits x≤0 and x≥1, where H₀ has zero density and H₁ has positive density.

D.why: This is also incomplete and uses the wrong cutoff within the null support.

items.repaired: The scan marks A and C. Statement C is incomplete as a full rejection region; the correct region also rejects outside the null support.

items.stem: Under H₀, X has density 1/2 on (−1,1); under H₁, X has density 1−|x| on (−1,1). At level α, 0<α<1, which combination of statements is true? Statements: (A) an MP test exists for every α; (B) an MP test fails to exist for some α; (C) reject H₀ when −α≤X≤α.
items.explanation: The likelihood ratio on (−1,1) is f₁(x)/f₀(x)=2(1−|x|), which is largest near zero and decreases as |x| increases. The Neyman–Pearson test therefore rejects for |X|≤c. Under H₀, X is Uniform(−1,1), so P₀(|X|≤c)=c; choosing c=α gives a level-α test. Thus an MP test exists for every α, and its rejection region is −α≤X≤α. Statements A and C are true.
items.repaired: The scan contains three statements; the four standard combination options were added to fit the app's single-choice format.

items.stem: For an iid sample from f(x;θ)=θx^(θ−1), 0<x<1, θ>0, which statements are correct?
statements: The product ΠXᵢ is sufficient for θ.
The sum Σln(Xᵢ) is sufficient for θ.
items.explanation: The likelihood is L(θ)=θⁿ(ΠXᵢ)^(θ−1), so the data enter through ΠXᵢ; equivalently they enter through Σln(Xᵢ). Both are one-to-one transformations and are sufficient. The log-likelihood is n ln θ+(θ−1)Σln(Xᵢ); setting its derivative n/θ+Σln(Xᵢ)=0 gives θ̂=−n/Σln(Xᵢ). Finally E(X)=θ/(θ+1). Equating this to X̄ and solving gives θ̃=X̄/(1−X̄). All four statements are true.

A.why: The factorisation theorem shows that the product is sufficient.

B.why: The sum of logarithms is a one-to-one transformation of the product.

C.why: Solving the likelihood score equation gives −n divided by the log-sum.

D.why: Solving X̄=θ/(θ+1) gives θ=X̄/(1−X̄).

items.repaired: The scan marks A, B and C but not D. The moment equation confirms D is also true; the bank corrects the incomplete source marking.

items.stem: Let X be a single observation from a Poisson distribution with parameter λ. Which option gives an unbiased estimator of 1/λ?
options: An unbiased estimator does not exist
items.explanation: For one observation X~Poisson(λ), an unbiased estimator would be a function g(X) satisfying E[g(X)]=1/λ for every λ>0. But E[g(X)]=e^(−λ)Σₓ₌₀∞g(x)λˣ/x!, so after multiplying by e^λ the left side is a power series containing only nonnegative powers of λ. The target e^λ/λ contains a λ^(−1) term. These cannot agree for every λ>0. Thus no unbiased estimator of 1/λ exists from one Poisson observation. Option D is correct.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Uniform(θ₁,θ₂), where θ₁<θ₂, and let s²=(1/(n−1))Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)². Which are the method-of-moments estimators of θ₁ and θ₂?
items.explanation: For Uniform(θ₁,θ₂), the population mean is (θ₁+θ₂)/2 and the population variance is (θ₂−θ₁)²/12. The method of moments equates the mean to X̄ and the variance to the second central sample moment (1/n)Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)². Since s² uses denominator n−1, this central moment is ((n−1)/n)s². Therefore θ₂−θ₁=√[12(n−1)s²/n]. Combining this width with the midpoint X̄ gives θ̂₁=X̄−√[3(n−1)s²/n] and θ̂₂=X̄+√[3(n−1)s²/n]. Statements B and C are correct.

A.why: The upper endpoint estimate must be above the sample mean, not below it.

B.why: The lower endpoint is the sample mean minus half the estimated width.

C.why: The upper endpoint is the sample mean plus half the estimated width.

D.why: The lower endpoint estimate must be below the sample mean, not above it.

items.repaired: The scan uses a sample-variance symbol with compressed typography; the formula is transcribed as s²=(1/(n−1))Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)², matching the printed denominator.

items.stem: Under H₀, X has density f₀(x)=2x for 0<x<1; under H₁, X has density f₁(x)=4x³ for 0<x<1. For a most powerful test of size 0.1 that rejects H₀ when 2X²>k, what is its power?
items.explanation: The likelihood ratio is f₁(x)/f₀(x)=2x², which increases with x, so the most powerful test rejects for large X. The size condition is P₀(2X²>k)=0.1. Under H₀, F₀(x)=x², so 1−k/2=0.1 and k/2=0.9. Under H₁, F₁(x)=x⁴. Hence the power is P₁(2X²>k)=1−(√(k/2))⁴=1−(k/2)²=1−0.9²=0.19. Option A is correct.

items.stem: In a sample of 1,000 people, 540 prefer rice and 460 prefer wheat. To test whether the two foods are equally popular, find the large-sample z statistic for H₀:p=0.5.
items.explanation: The sample proportion of rice eaters is p̂=540/1000=0.54. Under H₀:p=0.5, the standard error is √[p₀(1−p₀)/n]=√[0.5×0.5/1000]=√0.00025≈0.01581. Therefore z=(p̂−p₀)/SE=(0.54−0.50)/0.01581≈2.5298, which rounds to 2.532 in the printed options. Option D is correct. For a two-sided 1% test, this is slightly below the usual critical value 2.576, so the null would not be rejected at that level.

items.stem: Which statements about estimators are correct?
statements: An estimator can be unbiased but not consistent.
An estimator can be biased but consistent.
A sufficient estimator is always unbiased.
An UMVU estimator is always unbiased.
items.explanation: Unbiasedness concerns the estimator's expectation at each sample size, while consistency concerns convergence as the sample size grows. An estimator such as T_n=X₁ for estimating a population mean can be unbiased but fail to become more concentrated, so A is possible. The usual sample variance with denominator n is biased for finite n but consistent, so B is possible. Sufficiency describes how the sample contains information about the parameter; it does not by itself guarantee unbiasedness, so C is false. UMVU means uniformly minimum-variance unbiased, so unbiasedness is part of its definition and D is true. Hence A, B and D are correct.

A.why: The estimator X₁ remains unbiased but its variance does not shrink with n.

B.why: The sample variance with denominator n is biased at finite n but converges to the population variance.

C.why: Sufficiency and unbiasedness are different properties.

D.why: Unbiasedness is part of the definition of UMVU.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from Uniform(0,θ), θ>0. Which of the following estimators are consistent for θ?
items.explanation: For a Uniform(0,θ) sample, the sample maximum T₁ approaches θ as the sample size grows; in fact, T₁ converges almost surely to θ. Since (n+1)/n tends to one, multiplying T₁ by this factor does not change its probability limit, so T₂ is also consistent. The population mean is θ/2. By the law of large numbers, X̄ converges in probability to θ/2, so 2X̄ converges in probability to θ. Therefore all three estimators are consistent.

A.why: The sample maximum converges almost surely to the upper endpoint θ.

B.why: The multiplier (n+1)/n tends to one, preserving the limit θ.

C.why: The sample mean converges to E(X)=θ/2, so twice it converges to θ.

D.why: All three estimators listed are consistent.

items.repaired: The source lists the estimators separately but has no 'all of these' option. The multi-select combination format expresses that all three are consistent.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from f(x;θ)=θx^(θ−1), 0<x<1, θ>0. Which statements are correct?
statements: The maximum likelihood estimator is θ̂=−n/Σᵢ₌₁ⁿln Xᵢ.
The Fisher information per observation is I(θ)=1/θ².
The maximum likelihood estimator is θ̂=−n/Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ(ln Xᵢ)².
The Fisher information per observation is I(θ)=−1/θ².
items.explanation: The likelihood is L(θ)=θⁿ∏Xᵢ^(θ−1). Its log is ℓ(θ)=n lnθ+(θ−1)ΣlnXᵢ. Differentiate: ℓ′(θ)=n/θ+ΣlnXᵢ. Setting this equal to zero gives θ̂=−n/ΣlnXᵢ, so A is correct. The second derivative for one observation is −1/θ², so the Fisher information is the negative expected second derivative, 1/θ². Thus B is correct. The denominator in C must be the sum of logarithms, not squared logarithms, and information is nonnegative, so D is false.

A.why: Solving the likelihood score equation gives θ̂=−n/ΣlnXᵢ.

B.why: The negative expected second derivative of one-observation log likelihood is 1/θ².

C.why: The score contains ΣlnXᵢ, not Σ(lnXᵢ)².

D.why: Fisher information is positive here: 1/θ².

items.stem: A random sample X₁,…,Xₙ is drawn from f(x;θ)=Γ(3+θ)/[Γ(3)Γ(θ)]·x²(1−x)^(θ−1), 0<x<1, θ>0. Which statistic is sufficient for θ?
items.explanation: The joint likelihood is proportional to [Γ(3+θ)/(Γ(3)Γ(θ))]ⁿ × (∏Xᵢ²) × (∏(1−Xᵢ))^(θ−1). The factor ∏Xᵢ² does not involve θ. All dependence on θ and the sample is through T=∏(1−Xᵢ). By the factorisation theorem, T is sufficient for θ. Option A is correct.

items.stem: For iid observations from the zero-truncated Poisson distribution P(X=x)=e^(−λ)λˣ/[(1−e^(−λ))x!], x=1,2,…, find the Cramér–Rao lower bound for the variance of an unbiased estimator of λ based on n observations.
items.explanation: For one observation, log f(X;λ)=−λ+Xlnλ−ln(1−e^(−λ))−ln(X!). Its score is X/λ−1/(1−e^(−λ)). The Fisher information can be written as Var(X)/λ². For a zero-truncated Poisson variable, Var(X)=λ/(1−e^(−λ))−λ²e^(−λ)/(1−e^(−λ))². Simplifying gives I(λ)=[1−e^(−λ)−λe^(−λ)]/[λ(1−e^(−λ))²]. For n independent observations, information is nI(λ), so the Cramér–Rao bound is 1/[nI(λ)], which is option A.

items.stem: In a sample of 257 randomly selected students, 72 work as university faculty. Using the normal approximation, construct a 99% confidence interval for the population proportion, expressed as percentages.
items.explanation: The sample proportion is p̂=72/257≈0.2802. The standard error is √[p̂(1−p̂)/257]≈0.0280. For a 99% two-sided confidence interval, z_(0.995)≈2.576. Thus p̂±2.576(SE)=0.2802±2.576(0.0280), giving approximately (0.2080,0.3523), or (20.80%,35.23%). This matches option C after rounding.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from the Laplace density f(x;σ)=(1/(2σ))e^(−|x|/σ), x∈R, σ>0. What is the UMVU estimator of σʳ, for r>0?
items.explanation: For a Laplace(0,σ) variable, |Xᵢ| has an exponential distribution with scale σ. Hence T=Σ|Xᵢ| has a Gamma distribution with shape n and scale σ, and E(Tʳ)=σʳΓ(n+r)/Γ(n). The statistic T is complete and sufficient for σ in this one-parameter exponential family. Therefore Tʳ divided by Γ(n+r)/Γ(n) is unbiased and, by the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem, is the UMVU estimator: [Γ(n)/Γ(n+r)](Σ|Xᵢ|)ʳ. Option D is correct.

items.stem: A random sample of size n is drawn from Uniform(0,θ), and γ is the sample range. Let ξ be defined by ξ^(n−1)[n−(n−1)ξ]=α, where 0<α<1. What is the confidence interval for θ with confidence coefficient 1−α?
items.explanation: For a Uniform(0,θ) sample, the sample range R satisfies P(R/θ≤ξ)=ξ^(n−1)[n−(n−1)ξ]. By the definition of ξ, this probability is α. Therefore P(R/θ>ξ)=1−α. Also R/θ≤1 because the range cannot exceed θ. Combining these gives ξ<R/θ≤1, which rearranges to R<θ<R/ξ. Thus the confidence interval is (γ,γ/ξ), option C.

items.stem: A discrete random variable X has PMF under H₀ and H₁ as follows: for x=1,…,6, f₀(x)=(0.01,0.01,0.01,0.01,0.01,0.95) and f₁(x)=(0.05,0.04,0.03,0.02,0.01,0.85). For a Neyman–Pearson test of size α=0.03, what are the critical region and type II error β?
items.explanation: The likelihood ratio is λ(x)=f₁(x)/f₀(x). Its values for x=1,…,6 are 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0.85/0.95≈0.895. The Neyman–Pearson rule rejects H₀ for the largest likelihood ratios. Under H₀, the probability of x=1,2,3 is 0.01+0.01+0.01=0.03, giving the required size. The type II error is the probability under H₁ of not rejecting, which is P₁(X=4,5,6)=0.02+0.01+0.85=0.88. Option A is correct.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from the discrete uniform distribution P(X=x;N)=1/N, x=1,2,…,N. If T=max(X₁,…,Xₙ), what is the UMVU estimator of N?
items.explanation: For T=max(X₁,…,Xₙ), P(T=t)=[tⁿ−(t−1)ⁿ]/Nⁿ, t=1,…,N. Define h(t)=[t^(n+1)−(t−1)^(n+1)]/[tⁿ−(t−1)ⁿ]. Then E[h(T)]=(1/Nⁿ)Σₜ₌₁ᴺ[t^(n+1)−(t−1)^(n+1)]. This sum telescopes to N^(n+1)/Nⁿ=N, so h(T) is unbiased. The maximum T is sufficient and complete for N in this family, hence the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem makes h(T) the UMVU estimator. Option B is correct.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from Uniform(0,θ), θ>0, and let X₍ₙ₎ be the maximum likelihood estimator of θ. What is the limiting distribution of Yₙ=n(θ−X₍ₙ₎)?
items.explanation: For y≥0, P(Yₙ>y)=P(n(θ−X₍ₙ₎)>y)=P(X₍ₙ₎<θ−y/n). Since the sample is iid Uniform(0,θ), this probability is [(θ−y/n)/θ]ⁿ=(1−y/(nθ))ⁿ. As n→∞, it tends to e^(−y/θ), the survival function of an exponential distribution with rate 1/θ (equivalently, mean θ). Thus option A is correct.

items.stem: Let X₁~Binomial(n₁,p) and X₂~Binomial(n₂,p) be independent. Find E(X₁ | X₁+X₂=a).
items.explanation: Think of X₁ and X₂ as counts of successes in two independent groups containing n₁ and n₂ Bernoulli trials, all with the same success probability p. Given that the total number of successes is a, the a success positions are equally likely among the n₁+n₂ trial positions. The expected number falling in the first group is a times the fraction n₁/(n₁+n₂). Therefore E(X₁|X₁+X₂=a)=a n₁/(n₁+n₂), option A.

items.stem: A random sample from Bernoulli(p), 0<p<1, is 0, 0, 0, 1, 0. Find the maximum likelihood estimator of p.
items.explanation: For Bernoulli observations, the likelihood is p^(number of ones)(1−p)^(number of zeros). The maximum likelihood estimator is the sample proportion of ones. There is one success in five observations, so p̂=1/5. Option C is correct.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid N(2θ,θ²), θ>0. Which estimator is consistent for θ?
items.explanation: For X~N(2θ,θ²), E(X²)=Var(X)+[E(X)]²=θ²+4θ²=5θ². By the weak law of large numbers, (1/n)ΣXᵢ² converges in probability to 5θ². Dividing by 5 and taking the square root gives an estimator converging in probability to θ. Therefore option B is consistent.

items.stem: For a normal population with unknown variance, a 100(1−α)% confidence interval for μ is constructed as X̄±t_{α/2,n−1}S/√n. What is the probability that this interval contains μ?
items.explanation: The Student t pivot T=(X̄−μ)/(S/√n) has a t distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom. By the definition of the two-sided critical value t_{α/2,n−1}, P(−t_{α/2,n−1}≤T≤t_{α/2,n−1})=1−α. This event is exactly that the stated confidence interval contains μ. Therefore the coverage probability is 1−α, option A.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid from the Laplace density f_θ(x)=(1/(2θ))e^(−|x|/θ), x∈R, θ>0. For testing H₀:θ=1 against H₁:θ=2, what is the form of the most powerful critical region?
items.explanation: The likelihood ratio is L(2)/L(1)=(1/2)ⁿexp[(1/2)Σ|Xᵢ|]. This is an increasing function of Σ|Xᵢ|. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the most powerful test rejects H₀ for large likelihood ratios, so the critical region has the form Σ|Xᵢ|>k. Option A is correct.

items.stem: A sample −1, 0, 1, 2, −10 is drawn from a double-exponential (Laplace) distribution with unknown location μ and scale σ. Find the maximum likelihood estimate of σ.
items.explanation: For the Laplace distribution, the MLE of the location μ is the sample median. The sorted sample is −10,−1,0,1,2, so μ̂=0. The MLE of the scale is the mean absolute deviation from this median: σ̂=(1/5)(10+1+0+1+2)=14/5=2.8.
items.check: Median is 0; average absolute deviation is (10+1+0+1+2)/5=2.8.

items.stem: Consider the simple linear regression model Yᵢ=β₀+β₁xᵢ+εᵢ, i=1,…,n, with fixed xᵢ and independent errors εᵢ~N(0,σ²). Which statements about the least-squares estimators are correct?
items.explanation: These are the standard least-squares formulas in simple linear regression with fixed design and independent homoscedastic errors. The slope estimator is the cross-product divided by Sxx. Its variance is σ²/Sxx. The intercept variance is σ²(1/n+x̄²/Sxx), and the covariance between intercept and slope estimators is −x̄σ²/Sxx. Thus all four statements are correct.

A.why: This is the usual least-squares slope formula.

B.why: The slope variance is σ²/Sxx, where Sxx=Σ(xᵢ−x̄)².

C.why: The intercept variance is σ²[1/n+x̄²/Sxx].

D.why: The intercept-slope covariance is −x̄σ²/Sxx.

items.stem: Consider the simple linear regression model Yᵢ=β₀+β₁xᵢ+εᵢ, where β₀ is known. Find the ordinary least-squares estimator of β₁.
items.explanation: Since β₀ is known, minimise Q(β₁)=Σ[Yᵢ−β₀−β₁xᵢ]². Differentiate with respect to β₁ and set the derivative to zero: −2Σxᵢ(Yᵢ−β₀−β₁xᵢ)=0. Rearranging gives β̂₁=Σxᵢ(Yᵢ−β₀)/Σxᵢ². Option A is correct.

items.stem: In the simple linear regression model Yᵢ=β₀+β₁xᵢ+εᵢ, suppose E(εᵢ)=0 and Var(εᵢ)=σᵢ² are known and may differ across observations. What is the weighted least-squares estimator of β₁ when an intercept is included?
items.explanation: Weighted least squares minimises Σwᵢ(Yᵢ−β₀−β₁xᵢ)², where wᵢ=1/σᵢ². After eliminating the intercept using weighted means x̄_w=Σwᵢxᵢ/Σwᵢ and Ȳ_w=ΣwᵢYᵢ/Σwᵢ, the slope estimator is the weighted covariance divided by the weighted sum of squared deviations: β̂₁=Σwᵢ(xᵢ−x̄_w)(Yᵢ−Ȳ_w)/Σwᵢ(xᵢ−x̄_w)². Option A is correct.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from N(μ,1). Find the maximum likelihood estimator of μ.
items.explanation: The likelihood is proportional to exp[−(1/2)Σ(Xᵢ−μ)²]. Maximising it is equivalent to minimising Σ(Xᵢ−μ)². Differentiating with respect to μ and setting the result to zero gives μ̂=(1/n)ΣXᵢ=X̄. Option A is correct.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₖ be a random sample from Binomial(n,p), where n is known. Find the maximum likelihood estimator of p.
items.explanation: The likelihood is proportional to p^(ΣXᵢ)(1−p)^(kn−ΣXᵢ). The log-likelihood derivative is ΣXᵢ/p−(kn−ΣXᵢ)/(1−p). Setting it to zero gives p̂=ΣXᵢ/(kn)=X̄/n. Option B is correct.

items.stem: Suppose Y~Binomial(2,p). Four independent observations are 1, 2, 0 and 2. Find the maximum likelihood estimate of p.
items.explanation: The total number of successes is 1+2+0+2=5, and the total number of Bernoulli trials is 4×2=8. The binomial likelihood is maximised at the sample proportion p̂=5/8=0.625, which rounds to 0.63. Option C is correct.

items.stem: Let X~Uniform(0,θ). For testing H₀:θ=1 against H₁:θ=2, the critical region is 1<X<1.5. Find the level of the test.
items.explanation: The level is the probability of rejection under H₀. Under H₀, X~Uniform(0,1), so X is never strictly greater than 1. Thus P₀(1<X<1.5)=0, and the test level is zero. Option C is correct.

items.stem: A single observation has density fθ(x)=θx^(θ−1), 0<x<1. For testing H₀:θ=3 against H₁:θ=2, find k so that the most powerful critical region X<k has significance level 0.08.
items.explanation: The likelihood ratio f₂(x)/f₃(x)=(2x)/(3x²)=2/(3x) is largest for small x, so the most powerful critical region is X<k. Under H₀, the CDF is F₃(k)=k³. The significance condition is P₃(X<k)=k³=0.08. Hence k=0.08^(1/3)≈0.4309, or 0.431. Option B is correct.

items.stem: A sample of size 16 is drawn from a normal population with variance 16. Test H₀:μ=10 against H₁:μ=15 at significance level 0.05. Given z₀.₉₅=1.645, find the most powerful critical region.
items.explanation: The population standard deviation is 4, so the standard error of X̄ is 4/√16=1. For the one-sided alternative μ=15>10, reject H₀ for large values of X̄. The 5% upper-tail critical value under H₀ is 10+1.645(1)=11.645. Thus the most powerful critical region is X̄>11.645, option B.

items.stem: A sample of size 16 is drawn from a normal population with known variance 16. Test H₀: μ=10 against H₁: μ=15 at significance level 0.05. Given z₀.₉₅=1.645, the power of the most powerful test is which of the following, where Φ is the standard normal CDF?
items.explanation: The standard error of the sample mean is σ/√n=4/4=1. For the upper-tailed test, reject H₀ when X̄>10+1.645(1)=11.645. Under H₁, X̄ has mean 15 and standard deviation 1. Therefore power=P₁₅(X̄>11.645)=P[Z>(11.645−15)]=P(Z>−3.355)=Φ(3.355), approximately Φ(3.36). Option C is correct.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid with density f(x|θ)=(log θ)θˣ/(θ−1), 0<x<1, where θ>1 is unknown. The statistic T=Σᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ is:
items.explanation: The joint density is [(log θ)/(θ−1)]ⁿ θ^(Σxᵢ) on the sample space 0<xᵢ<1. By the factorisation theorem, the sample enters the parameter-dependent part only through T=ΣXᵢ, so T is sufficient. Write η=log θ, whose parameter space is η>0, an open interval. The joint density is a full one-parameter exponential family with fixed support and open natural-parameter space; its natural statistic T is complete. Hence T is complete and sufficient.

items.stem: A single observation X has density f(x|θ)=e^(x−θ)/[1+e^(x−θ)]², −∞<x<∞, where θ is an unknown location parameter. For testing H₀: θ≤θ₀ against H₁: θ>θ₀, a UMP test of size α rejects when:
options: X>k, where k is chosen so that Pθ₀(X>k)=α.
X<k, where k is chosen so that Pθ₀(X>k)=α.
X>k, where k is chosen so that Pθ₀(X<k)=α.
X<k, where k is chosen so that Pθ₀(X<k)=α.
items.explanation: This is a logistic location family. As θ increases, the distribution shifts to the right, and the likelihood ratio for a larger θ against θ₀ is increasing in x. Thus the family has a monotone likelihood ratio in X. The Karlin–Rubin principle gives an upper-tail rejection region X>k. To make the test have size α at the boundary θ=θ₀, choose k so that Pθ₀(X>k)=α.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid with density f(x|θ)=θ/x^(θ+1), x>1, where θ>1 is unknown. Which estimator is consistent for θ?
items.explanation: For this Pareto density, set U=log X. Then P(U>u)=P(X>eᵘ)=e^(−θu), so U is exponential with rate θ and E(log X)=1/θ. By the law of large numbers, (1/n)Σlog Xᵢ converges in probability to 1/θ. Taking its reciprocal gives n/Σlog Xᵢ→θ, so option D is consistent.

items.stem: Let X have density f(x|θ)=2x/θ² for 0<x<θ, where θ>0 is unknown. Which of the following are exact 100(1−α)% confidence intervals for θ, for 0<α<1?
items.explanation: Let U=X/θ. Its CDF is P(U≤u)=u² for 0<u<1. For interval A, coverage is P(X≤θ≤X/√α)=P(√α≤U≤1)=1−α. For interval C, coverage is P(√(2/(2−α))X≤θ≤√(2/α)X)=P(√(α/2)≤U≤√((2−α)/2))=(2−α)/2−α/2=1−α. Interval B has coverage 3/4, independent of α, and interval D has zero coverage because X<θ almost surely. Thus A and C only are valid.

A.why: Using U=X/θ with CDF u², the interval's coverage is 1−α.

B.why: The coverage is P(1/2≤U≤1)=1−1/4=3/4, not 1−α for general α.

C.why: Its coverage is (2−α)/2−α/2=1−α.

D.why: Since X<θ almost surely, θ cannot lie in [0,X].

items.stem: The average three-year growth of an established variety of pine trees is 10.1 inches. A biologist claims a new variety has greater three-year growth. A random sample of 25 new trees has mean growth 10.8 inches. Which null and alternative hypotheses test the claim?
items.explanation: The reference value is the established population mean, 10.1 inches, not the observed sample mean 10.8. The claim is that the new variety has a greater population mean, so the alternative is μ>10.1. The null is stated at the boundary value μ=10.1. The sample mean is evidence used by the test; it is not the hypothesised mean.

items.stem: Which statement about hypothesis testing is false?
options: The critical region contains test-statistic values for which the null hypothesis is rejected.
The significance level is the probability of a Type I error.
For H₁: μ>μ₀, large values of the sample mean provide evidence against H₀.
The p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
items.explanation: A p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true; it is the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one. It is not the probability that H₀ itself is true. The other statements are standard definitions. For a two-sided alternative, the rejection region has two tails.

items.stem: Which statement gives a correct interpretation of a p-value?
options: A very small p-value means the observed result, or a more extreme one, would be unusual if H₀ were true.
The p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
The p-value is the probability of making a Type II error.
A larger p-value always gives stronger evidence against H₀.
items.explanation: The p-value is computed under the assumption that H₀ is true. It measures how unusual the observed test statistic is, counting results at least as extreme in the direction(s) specified by the test. A small p-value is evidence against H₀. It is not the probability that H₀ is true and is not the Type II error probability.

items.stem: Which statement about sampling distributions and statistical inference is false?
options: The sampling distribution of the sample mean has the same standard deviation as the original population.
The sampling distribution of the sample mean has the same mean as the original population, when the mean exists.
If the original population is normal, the sample mean is normally distributed.
Inferential statistics uses sample information to draw conclusions about a population.
items.explanation: For iid observations with population standard deviation σ, the standard deviation of the sample mean is σ/√n, not σ (unless n=1). The sample mean is unbiased, so its expectation equals the population mean. A sample mean from a normal population is exactly normal, and using sample information to draw conclusions about a population is the purpose of inferential statistics.

items.stem: Let N be the number of heads in 100 independent tosses of a coin. For testing H₀:p=0.5 against H₁:p>0.5 at the 5% significance level, using the exact binomial test, which rejection region is appropriate?
items.explanation: Under H₀, N~Binomial(100,0.5). For an upper-tail test, choose the smallest integer cutoff whose upper-tail probability is no more than 0.05. The exact binomial probabilities give P(N≥59)≈0.0443, whereas P(N≥58)≈0.0666. Thus the non-randomised 5% rejection region is N≥59, equivalently N>58. The test rejects only for sufficiently many heads.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid with density f(x|θ)=θx^(θ−1), 0<x<1, θ>0. The Cramér–Rao lower bound for the variance of an unbiased estimator of θ is:
items.explanation: For one observation, the log-likelihood is log θ+(θ−1)log x. Its score is 1/θ+log X. Under this density, E(log X)=−1/θ and Var(log X)=1/θ², so the Fisher information from one observation is 1/θ². For n independent observations, information is n/θ². The Cramér–Rao lower bound is the reciprocal information, θ²/n. Thus the variance of any unbiased estimator cannot be below θ²/n under the regularity conditions.

items.stem: An estimator Tₙ of a parameter θ is consistent if, for every ε>0:
items.explanation: Consistency means that the estimator gets arbitrarily close to the true parameter with probability approaching one as the sample size increases. Formally, Tₙ converges in probability to θ if, for every fixed ε>0, P(|Tₙ−θ|>ε) tends to zero as n tends to infinity. Equivalently, P(|Tₙ−θ|≤ε) tends to one. This is exactly option D.

items.stem: Suppose X has a Gamma distribution with shape β and scale θ, with density f(x)=x^(β−1)e^(−x/θ)/[θ^βΓ(β)] for x≥0. Using the first two raw sample moments m′₁ and m′₂, the method-of-moments estimator of β is:
items.explanation: For a Gamma(shape β, scale θ) distribution, E(X)=βθ and E(X²)=β(β+1)θ². Hence Var(X)=E(X²)−[E(X)]²=βθ². Dividing [E(X)]² by Var(X) gives β²θ²/(βθ²)=β. The method of moments replaces E(X) by m′₁ and E(X²) by m′₂, so β̂=(m′₁)²/[m′₂−(m′₁)²]. This is option C.

items.stem: A single observation X comes from a Uniform(θ,θ+1) distribution. To test H₀:θ=0 against H₁:θ=1/2, consider the test that rejects H₀ when X>2/3. What is the power of this test?
items.explanation: Power is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when the alternative is true. Under H₁, θ=1/2, so X~Uniform(1/2,3/2), whose interval has length 1. The rejection event is X>2/3. Its probability is the length of (2/3,3/2) divided by 1: 3/2−2/3=9/6−4/6=5/6. Therefore the power is 5/6.

items.stem: Under H₀, a discrete random variable X has probabilities P(X=0,1,2,3)=(0.4,0.3,0.2,0.1). Under H₁, they are (0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4). Consider the test that rejects H₀ when X>3/2. What are the size α and power β?
items.explanation: The rejection region X>3/2 consists of X=2 or X=3. Under H₀, its probability is 0.2+0.1=0.3, which is the size α. Under H₁, its probability is 0.3+0.4=0.7, which is the power β. Thus α=0.3 and β=0.7.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from the exponential density f(x;θ)=θe^(−θx), x>0, θ>0. What is the method-of-moments estimator of θ?
items.explanation: For an exponential distribution with rate θ, E(X)=1/θ. Equate the first population moment to the sample mean: X̄=1/θ. Solving gives θ̂=1/X̄=n/ΣXᵢ. This is the method-of-moments estimator.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample with mean μ and finite variance σ². Define Tₙ=2Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ iXᵢ/[n(n+1)]. For estimating μ, Tₙ is:
items.explanation: The weights sum to one because 2Σi/[n(n+1)]=1, so E(Tₙ)=μ and Tₙ is unbiased. Independence gives Var(Tₙ)=4σ²Σi²/[n²(n+1)²]=2σ²(2n+1)/[3n(n+1)], which tends to zero. Thus Tₙ converges in mean square, hence in probability, to μ and is consistent.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Bernoulli(θ), and let T=ΣXᵢ. What is the UMVUE of g(θ)=θ(1−θ) in terms of T?
items.explanation: T has a Binomial(n,θ) distribution, so E[T(n−T)]=n(n−1)θ(1−θ). Therefore T(n−T)/[n(n−1)]=(nT−T²)/[n(n−1)] is unbiased. Since T is complete and sufficient for θ in the Bernoulli family, the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem makes this unbiased function of T the UMVUE.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Uniform(0,θ), θ>0. Which statement is correct?
options: The sample maximum X₍ₙ₎ is an unbiased estimator of θ.
The sample maximum X₍ₙ₎ is the maximum likelihood estimator of θ.
The sample minimum X₍₁₎ is the maximum likelihood estimator of θ.
(n+1)X₍ₙ₎ is an unbiased estimator of θ.
items.explanation: The likelihood is proportional to θ^(−n) for θ≥X₍ₙ₎ and zero otherwise. It decreases as θ increases, so its maximum occurs at the smallest allowed value, θ̂=X₍ₙ₎. However, E[X₍ₙ₎]=nθ/(n+1), so the maximum is biased downward. The unbiased correction is (n+1)X₍ₙ₎/n, not (n+1)X₍ₙ₎.

items.stem: Let X₁,X₂,X₃ be independent observations from N(θ,1). Define T₁=(X₁+X₂+2X₃)/4 and T₂=(X₁+X₂+X₃)/3. What is the efficiency of T₁ relative to T₂?
items.explanation: Both estimators are unbiased because their coefficients sum to one. Var(T₁)=(1+1+4)/16=3/8, while Var(T₂)=(1+1+1)/9=1/3. The efficiency of T₁ relative to T₂ is Var(T₂)/Var(T₁)=(1/3)/(3/8)=8/9.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be independent observations from Uniform(0,θ), where θ is restricted to the positive integers. What is the maximum likelihood estimator of θ?
options: The greatest integer less than or equal to X₍ₙ₎.
The smallest integer greater than or equal to X₍ₙ₎.
items.explanation: The likelihood is θ^(−n) when θ≥X₍ₙ₎ and zero otherwise. Since θ must be a positive integer and the likelihood decreases as θ increases, choose the smallest integer that is at least the sample maximum. This is the ceiling of X₍ₙ₎.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid N(0,σ²). For testing H₀: σ=1 against H₁: σ=2, the most powerful test rejects H₀ when which statistic exceeds a critical constant c?
items.explanation: The joint likelihood under σ is proportional to σ^(−n) exp{−ΣXᵢ²/(2σ²)}. The likelihood ratio L(σ=2)/L(σ=1) is 2^(−n) exp{(3/8)ΣXᵢ²}, which increases as ΣXᵢ² increases. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the most powerful test rejects for large values of ΣXᵢ². The known zero mean is why the raw sum of squares, not the centred sample sum of squares, is used.

items.stem: Suppose X₁,…,Xₙ are iid normal random variables with mean θ and variance θ, where θ>0. Which statistic is sufficient for θ?
options: Neither ΣXᵢ nor ΣXᵢ² is sufficient.
items.explanation: The joint density is proportional to θ^(−n/2) exp{−Σ(Xᵢ−θ)²/(2θ)}. Expand the square: the exponent is −ΣXᵢ²/(2θ)+ΣXᵢ−nθ/2. The factor exp(ΣXᵢ) does not involve θ and can be included in h(x). The remaining parameter-dependent part involves the sample only through ΣXᵢ². By the factorisation theorem, ΣXᵢ² is sufficient for θ.

items.stem: Three independent observations are taken from a Poisson distribution with parameter λ. If g(λ)=e^(−λ), what is the Cramér–Rao lower bound for the variance of an unbiased estimator of g(λ)?
items.explanation: For one Poisson(λ) observation, Fisher information is 1/λ. With three independent observations, total information is I(λ)=3/λ. The Cramér–Rao bound for an unbiased estimator of g(λ) is [g′(λ)]²/I(λ). Since g′(λ)=−e^(−λ), the bound is e^(−2λ)/(3/λ)=λe^(−2λ)/3.

items.stem: A random sample of size n is drawn from a normal population. Let s²=(1/n)Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)². Using the upper-tail chi-square critical-value convention P(χ²ᵥ>χ²_{α,ν})=α, which expression gives the 95% confidence interval for the population variance σ²?
items.explanation: For a normal population, Q=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/σ²=(n−1)S²/σ² has a chi-square distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom. Here s² is defined with divisor n, so Q=ns²/σ². Under the stated upper-tail convention, χ²_{0.025,n−1} is the larger critical value and χ²_{0.975,n−1} is the smaller. Inverting the central 95% probability statement gives ns²/χ²_{0.025,n−1} ≤ σ² ≤ ns²/χ²_{0.975,n−1}.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from a Gamma(α,β) population, where β>0 is known. For testing H₀: α=1 against H₁: α=2, the most powerful test rejects H₀ when which condition holds?
items.explanation: For the Gamma family with known scale/rate β, the likelihood ratio between shape 2 and shape 1 is a positive constant times ∏Xᵢ. Thus it is increasing in the product of the observations. The Neyman–Pearson lemma says to reject H₀ for large likelihood-ratio values, giving the region ∏Xᵢ>K. The sum is not the likelihood-ratio statistic for this simple-versus-simple comparison.

items.stem: A single observation X comes from an exponential distribution with mean 1/λ. Test H₀: λ=2 against H₁: λ=4 using the rejection region X≥3. What are the Type-I error probability α and Type-II error probability β?
items.explanation: For an exponential distribution with rate λ, P(X≥x)=e^(−λx). Under H₀ (λ=2), the Type-I error is the probability of rejecting: α=P₂(X≥3)=e^(−2×3)=e^(−6). Under H₁ (λ=4), the Type-II error is the probability of not rejecting: β=P₄(X<3)=1−P₄(X≥3)=1−e^(−4×3)=1−e^(−12).

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from a Poisson(θ) population and let T=ΣXᵢ. What is the UMVUE of θ²?
items.explanation: The sum T has a Poisson distribution with mean nθ. For a Poisson variable, E[T(T−1)]=(nθ)². Therefore E[T(T−1)/n²]=θ², so the proposed estimator is unbiased. Also T is complete and sufficient for θ in the Poisson family. By the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem, an unbiased function of this complete sufficient statistic is the unique UMVUE. Hence the answer is T(T−1)/n².

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from the Gamma density f(x)=αᵖx^(p−1)e^(−αx)/Γ(p), x>0, where p>0 is known and α>0 is unknown. Assume np>1. For the estimator α̂=p/X̄, what is E(α̂)?
items.explanation: Let S=ΣXᵢ=nX̄. Since each Xi is Gamma(shape p, rate α), S is Gamma(shape np, rate α). For a Gamma(k, rate α) variable with k>1, E(1/S)=α/(k−1). Therefore E(α̂)=E(np/S)=np·α/(np−1)=α/[1−1/(np)]. This is larger than α, so p/X̄ is biased upward. The condition np>1 is needed for this expectation to be finite; it is made explicit here because it is not printed in the source question.

items.stem: For an iid sample X₁,…,Xₙ from a population with mean μ and finite variance, consider E₁=[1/{n(n−1)}]Σ_{i≠j}XᵢXⱼ and E₂=X̄²−[1/{n(n−1)}]Σᵢ(Xᵢ−X̄)². Which statement about estimating μ² is correct?
options: E₁ is unbiased but E₂ is biased.
E₁ is biased but E₂ is unbiased.
Both E₁ and E₂ are unbiased.
Both E₁ and E₂ are biased.
items.explanation: For E₁, each product XiXj with i≠j has expectation E(Xi)E(Xj)=μ² by independence. There are n(n−1) ordered pairs, so E(E₁)=μ². For E₂, E(X̄²)=μ²+σ²/n. Also E[Σ(Xi−X̄)²]=(n−1)σ², so the expected correction term is (n−1)σ²/[n(n−1)]=σ²/n. Subtracting gives E(E₂)=μ². Both estimators are unbiased.

items.stem: A random sample X₁,…,Xₙ has density f(x;θ)=θ(1−x)^(θ−1), 0<x<1, θ>0. Which statistic is sufficient for θ?
items.explanation: The joint density is θⁿ∏(1−xᵢ)^(θ−1) on 0<xᵢ<1. Rewrite it as θⁿ exp{(θ−1)Σlog(1−xᵢ)} times the indicator of the fixed sample space. The sample enters the parameter-dependent part only through Σlog(1−Xᵢ). By the factorisation theorem, this statistic is sufficient for θ.

items.stem: Under H₀, X has density f₀(x)=1 for 0<x<1; under H₁, X has density f₁(x)=3x² for 0<x<1. A test rejects H₀ when X>0.85. What are the Type-I error probability and the power, respectively?
items.explanation: The Type-I error is P₀(X>0.85). Under H₀ the density is uniform on (0,1), so α=1−0.85=0.15. The power is P₁(X>0.85)=∫₀.₈₅¹3x²dx=[x³]₀.₈₅¹=1−(0.85)³. Therefore option C is correct.

items.stem: A random sample X₁,…,Xₙ has density f(x;θ)=(1+θ)x^θ for 0<x<1, where θ>−1. What is the maximum likelihood estimator of θ?
items.explanation: The likelihood is L(θ)=(1+θ)ⁿ∏Xᵢ^θ. Its log is ℓ(θ)=n log(1+θ)+θΣlog Xᵢ. Differentiate: ℓ′(θ)=n/(1+θ)+Σlog Xᵢ. Setting this to zero gives 1+θ̂=−n/(Σlog Xᵢ), so θ̂=−n/[log(∏Xᵢ)]−1. The second derivative is −n/(1+θ)²<0, confirming a maximum.

items.stem: Suppose L(X)≤U(X) for every x, Pθ(L(X)≤θ)=1−α₁ and Pθ(L(X)≤θ≤U(X))=1−α₁−α₂. What is Pθ(U(X)≥θ)?
items.explanation: Because L(X)≤U(X), the event U(X)<θ is contained in L(X)≤θ. The part of L(X)≤θ that is not covered by L(X)≤θ≤U(X) is exactly the event U(X)<θ, up to boundary conventions. Its probability is (1−α₁)−(1−α₁−α₂)=α₂. Hence Pθ(U(X)≥θ)=1−α₂.

items.stem: Two independent Bernoulli observations X₁,X₂ have success probability θ, with θ constrained to [1/3,2/3]. What is the maximum likelihood estimator of θ?
items.explanation: Without the constraint, the Bernoulli MLE is the sample proportion X̄=(X₁+X₂)/2. With θ restricted to [1/3,2/3], the constrained MLE is the projection of X̄ onto this interval. If X₁+X₂=0, the estimate is 1/3; if the sum is 1, it is 1/2; if the sum is 2, it is 2/3. The expression (2+X₁+X₂)/6 gives exactly these three values.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from N(μ,σ²). Define T₁=ΣXᵢ and T₂=ΣXᵢ². Which statement is correct about sufficiency for μ and σ²?
options: T₁ alone is sufficient for μ.
T₂ alone is sufficient for σ².
items.explanation: The joint normal likelihood is proportional to exp{−[ΣXᵢ²−2μΣXᵢ+nμ²]/(2σ²)} times a factor involving σ² and n. The data enter the parameter-dependent part only through ΣXᵢ and ΣXᵢ². By the factorisation theorem, the pair (T₁,T₂) is sufficient for (μ,σ²). Neither sum alone captures both sample features needed when both parameters are unknown.

items.stem: T₁ and T₂ are unbiased estimators of θ with variances v₁ and v₂, where v₁<v₂, and Cov(T₁,T₂)=v₁. Which statement about the estimator (T₁+T₂)/2 is correct?
options: It is more efficient than both T₁ and T₂.
It is more efficient than T₂ but less efficient than T₁.
It is more efficient than T₁.
It is more efficient than T₂ only if v₂>2v₁.
items.explanation: The average remains unbiased. Its variance is Var[(T₁+T₂)/2]=(1/4)[v₁+v₂+2Cov(T₁,T₂)]=(1/4)(3v₁+v₂). Since v₂>v₁, this is less than v₂. But it is greater than v₁ because (3v₁+v₂)/4>v₁ is equivalent to v₂>v₁. Thus the average is more efficient than T₂, but less efficient than T₁.

items.stem: Five independent observations from a density f(x;λ)=λ²x e^(−λx), x≥0, λ>0 are 5/3, 5/6, 5/12, 5/6 and 15/12. What is the maximum likelihood estimate of λ?
items.explanation: The likelihood is proportional to λ^(2n)exp(−λΣxᵢ), because the product of the xᵢ terms does not involve λ. The log-likelihood derivative is 2n/λ−Σxᵢ. Setting it to zero gives λ̂=2n/Σxᵢ. Here n=5 and the observations sum to 5, so λ̂=2(5)/5=2. The second derivative −2n/λ² is negative, confirming a maximum.

items.stem: Let X̄ be the sample mean from X₁,…,Xₙ drawn from a normal population with known mean 1 and unknown variance σ². What is the maximum likelihood estimator of σ²?
items.explanation: When the population mean is known to be 1, the normal likelihood is maximised by the average squared deviation from that known mean. Differentiating the log-likelihood with respect to σ² gives σ̂²=(1/n)Σ(Xᵢ−1)². The divisor is n, not n−1, because this is the maximum likelihood estimator rather than the unbiased sample variance.

items.stem: For a random sample from N(μ,σ²), let X̄ be the sample mean and s²=(1/(n−1))Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)². Which expression is an unbiased estimator of μ³?
items.explanation: For a normal sample, X̄ and s² are independent, E(s²)=σ², and E(X̄³)=μ³+3μσ²/n. Also E(X̄s²)=E(X̄)E(s²)=μσ². Therefore E[X̄³−3X̄s²/n]=μ³+3μσ²/n−3μσ²/n=μ³. So option C is unbiased.

items.stem: Let X be one observation from Uniform(θ,θ+1). For testing H₀: θ=1 against H₁: θ=2, reject H₀ when X>1.5. What are the power and size of this test, respectively?
items.explanation: Under H₀, X~Uniform(1,2), so P₁(X>1.5)=0.5; this is the size. Under H₁, X~Uniform(2,3), and every possible observation exceeds 1.5, so the rejection probability is 1. Therefore power=1 and size=1/2, option C.

items.stem: Let X be one observation from the discrete uniform distribution on {1,2,θ}, where θ∈{3,4}. To test H₀:θ=3 against H₁:θ=4, consider the test that rejects H₀ if X=4. What are the size and power of this test, respectively?
items.explanation: Under H₀, θ=3 and X is uniform on {1,2,3}, so X=4 is impossible and the size is zero. Under H₁, θ=4 and X is uniform on {1,2,4}; each value has probability 1/3. Therefore the power is P₄(X=4)=1/3. The size and power are 0 and 1/3.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from Bernoulli(p)=Binomial(1,p), where p∈(0,1), and suppose ΣXᵢ=n. What is the maximum likelihood estimate of p?
options: No MLE exists in the stated parameter space
items.explanation: The observed sample consists entirely of successes, so the likelihood is L(p)=pⁿ for 0<p<1. This function increases as p increases. Its supremum is 1 as p approaches 1, but p=1 is excluded from the parameter space (0,1). Therefore the likelihood has no maximiser inside the allowed parameter space, so an MLE does not exist as stated. If the parameter space included p=1, the MLE would be 1.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from N(θ,1), where θ is unknown and the variance is known. Which of the following statistics are sufficient for θ?

A.why: The factorisation theorem shows that the likelihood depends on θ through ΣXᵢ.

B.why: The tuple includes ΣXᵢ, so it retains the sufficient statistic.

C.why: This tuple also includes ΣXᵢ, so adding sample components does not remove sufficiency.

D.why: X̄ is a one-to-one rescaling of ΣXᵢ for fixed n.

items.explanation: The joint density is proportional to exp{−(1/2)Σ(Xᵢ−θ)²}. Expanding the square shows that its θ-dependent part is exp{θΣXᵢ−nθ²/2}. By the factorisation theorem, ΣXᵢ (equivalently X̄) is sufficient. Any statistic that includes ΣXᵢ as one of its components is also sufficient, because it retains all the information in that sufficient statistic. Hence all four listed statistics are sufficient.

items.stem: Let X~Uniform(θ,θ²), where θ∈{2,3}. Test H₀:θ=2 against H₁:θ=3 using the critical region X≥3.5. If α is the test size and β is its power, find α+β.
items.explanation: Under H₀, θ=2 and X is Uniform(2,4). The rejection region is X≥3.5, so α=P₂(X≥3.5)=(4−3.5)/(4−2)=1/4. Under H₁, θ=3 and X is Uniform(3,9). The power is β=P₃(X≥3.5)=(9−3.5)/(9−3)=5.5/6=11/12. Therefore α+β=1/4+11/12=3/12+11/12=14/12=7/6.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample with mean μ and finite variance. Define Tₙ=2Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ iXᵢ/[n(n+1)]. Which statement describes Tₙ as an estimator of μ?
items.explanation: First, E(Tₙ)=2μΣᵢ i/[n(n+1)]=2μ[n(n+1)/2]/[n(n+1)]=μ, so the estimator is unbiased. Since the observations are independent with common finite variance σ², Var(Tₙ)=4σ²Σᵢ i²/[n²(n+1)²]. Using Σi²=n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 gives Var(Tₙ)=2σ²(2n+1)/[3n(n+1)], which tends to zero. By Chebyshev's inequality, Tₙ converges in probability to μ, so it is consistent.

items.stem: Let X₁ and X₂ be iid Uniform(0,θ). Test H₀:θ=1 against H₁:θ=2. Which rejection rules have size at most 0.5 and power at least 0.5?

A.why: For θ=1 the size is 0 and for θ=2 the power is 1−(1.6/2)²=0.36, below 0.5.

B.why: For θ=1 the size is 0 and for θ=2 the power is P(X₁≥1,X₂≥1)=(1/2)²=0.25.

C.why: Under H₀ the size is P(X₁≥0.4)=0.6, which exceeds 0.5.

D.why: For iid continuous variables, P(X₁≥X₂)=1/2 under both hypotheses, so size and power are both 0.5.

items.explanation: Check size under θ=1 and power under θ=2. Rule 1 has size zero but power 1−(1.6/2)²=0.36. Rule 2 has size zero but power (1/2)²=0.25. Rule 3 has size P₁(X₁≥0.4)=0.6, too large. Rule 4 has probability 1/2 under either parameter because two iid continuous variables are equally likely to be in either order. Thus only rule 4 meets both requirements.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid N(0,σ²), where σ² is unknown. Which statistics are sufficient for σ²?

A.why: The likelihood depends on the sample through ΣXᵢ²; each listed statistic retains that sum or contains it as a function.

B.why: The vector of all squared observations determines their sum of squares.

C.why: ΣXᵢ² is the natural sufficient statistic for σ².

D.why: The sum of the two components is ΣXᵢ², so the pair retains the sufficient statistic.

items.explanation: The joint density is proportional to (σ²)^(−n/2) exp{−ΣXᵢ²/(2σ²)}. By the factorisation theorem, the sample enters the parameter-dependent part only through ΣXᵢ². The full sample and the vector of squares both determine this sum. The sum itself is sufficient, and the pair of partial sums also determines the total sum. Hence all four statistics are sufficient.

items.stem: A random sample is drawn from f(x;λ)=2λxe⁻ˡᵃᵐᵇᵈᵃˣ² for x>0, λ>0. Test H₀:λ=1/2 against H₁:λ=3/4 at level α. Which statements are correct?
statements: A most powerful test exists for every 0<α<1.
A most powerful test fails to exist for some α.
When it exists, the test rejects H₀ for small values of ΣXᵢ², i.e. ΣXᵢ²≤c.
When it exists, the test rejects H₀ for large values of ΣXᵢ², i.e. ΣXᵢ²≥c.
items.explanation: The hypotheses are simple: each specifies one value of λ. The Neyman–Pearson lemma therefore gives a most powerful level-α test for every α (with randomisation at a boundary if needed). For n observations, the likelihood is proportional to λⁿexp(−λΣXᵢ²). The likelihood ratio L(λ=3/4)/L(λ=1/2) is a positive constant times exp(−(1/4)ΣXᵢ²), which decreases as ΣXᵢ² increases. Evidence for H₁ is therefore strongest when the sum of squares is small, so the rejection region is ΣXᵢ²≤c. Statements A and C are true.

A.why: The Neyman–Pearson lemma applies to every pair of simple hypotheses.

B.why: A most powerful test exists at every level, allowing boundary randomisation.

C.why: The likelihood ratio decreases with the sum of squared observations.

D.why: Large sums of squares favour the smaller λ under H₀, not H₁.

items.stem: Let X be discrete uniform on {1,2,…,θ}, where θ∈{20,40}. Test H₀:θ=40 against H₁:θ=20 at significance level 0.1. The uniformly most powerful test rejects H₀ when:
items.explanation: Under H₀, X is uniform on 1,…,40; under H₁, it is uniform on 1,…,20. The likelihood ratio is 2 for x≤20 and 0 for x>20, so the Neyman–Pearson test rejects H₀ for the smallest observations. To obtain size 0.1 under H₀, choose the first four values because P₀(X≤4)=4/40=0.1. Therefore the rejection region is X≤4.

items.stem: A single observation X has an exponential distribution with mean 1/λ. Test H₀:λ=2 against H₁:λ=4 using rejection region X≥3. Find the Type I error α and Type II error β.
items.explanation: For an exponential distribution with rate λ, P(X≥x)=e⁻ˡᵃᵐᵇᵈᵃˣ. A Type I error occurs when H₀ is true but X≥3, so α=Pλ=2(X≥3)=e⁻⁶. A Type II error occurs when H₁ is true but the test does not reject, that is X<3. Under λ=4 this probability is 1−Pλ=4(X≥3)=1−e⁻¹². Thus option A is correct.

items.stem: A random sample X₁,…,Xₙ has density f(x;θ)=θxᶿ⁻¹ for 0≤x≤1, θ>0. Find the maximum likelihood estimator of θ.
items.explanation: The likelihood is L(θ)=θⁿ∏Xᵢᶿ⁻¹. Taking logs gives ℓ(θ)=n log θ+(θ−1)Σlog Xᵢ. Differentiate: ℓ′(θ)=n/θ+Σlog Xᵢ. Set this equal to zero to obtain θ̂=−n/Σlog Xᵢ. Since ℓ″(θ)=−n/θ²<0, this stationary point is a maximum. The answer is option A.

items.stem: A random sample X₁,…,Xₙ is drawn from f(x;θ)=2x/θ² for 0<x<θ. Find the method-of-moments estimator of θ.
items.explanation: The method of moments equates the population mean to the sample mean. First calculate E(X)=∫₀ᶿ x·(2x/θ²)dx=(2/θ²)(θ³/3)=2θ/3. Set this equal to X̄: X̄=2θ/3. Solving gives θ̂=3X̄/2=3ΣXᵢ/(2n), which is option A.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid with density f(x;θ)=θe⁻ᶿ⁽ˣ⁻¹⁾ for x≥1 and θ>0. Find the maximum likelihood estimator of θ.
items.explanation: The likelihood is L(θ)=θⁿ exp[−θΣ(Xᵢ−1)]. Its log is ℓ(θ)=n log θ−θΣ(Xᵢ−1). Differentiating gives ℓ′(θ)=n/θ−Σ(Xᵢ−1). Setting this to zero yields θ̂=n/Σ(Xᵢ−1)=1/(X̄−1). The second derivative is −n/θ²<0, confirming a maximum.

items.stem: A single observation X comes from Uniform(θ,θ+1). Test H₀:θ=0 against H₁:θ=1/2 using the rule that rejects H₀ when X>2/3. Find the power of this test.
items.explanation: Power is the probability of rejecting H₀ when H₁ is true. Under H₁, θ=1/2, so X is Uniform(1/2,3/2). The interval above 2/3 has length 3/2−2/3=5/6, while the full support has length 1. Therefore P(X>2/3|H₁)=5/6.

items.stem: A sample of size 7 is drawn from fθ(x)=(1+x²)/[3θ(1+θ²)] for −2θ≤x≤θ, θ>0. The observations are 12, −54, 26, −2, 24, 17, −39. Find the MLE of θ.
items.explanation: The likelihood is zero unless every observation lies in [−2θ,θ]. The largest observation is 26, so θ≥26. The smallest is −54, so −54≥−2θ, giving θ≥27. Hence the full sample is possible only when θ≥27. On this allowed range, the likelihood is proportional to [3θ(1+θ²)]⁻⁷, which decreases as θ increases. It is therefore maximised at the smallest allowed value, θ̂=27.

items.stem: Let X₁,X₂,X₃ be iid Normal(θ,θ²), with θ∈R unknown. Which estimators are unbiased for the stated targets?
options: Statements A, C and D only
items.explanation: For X~Normal(θ,θ²), E(X)=θ and E(X²)=Var(X)+[E(X)]²=2θ². Statement A has expectation (θ+2θ+3θ)/6=θ. Statement B has expectation (2θ²+4·2θ²+9·2θ²)/14=2θ², not θ². Statement C has expectation (2θ+2θ²)/2=θ+θ²=θ(1+θ). Statement D has expectation θ−(1/2)(2θ²)=θ−θ²=θ(1−θ). Therefore A, C and D are unbiased.

A.why: The coefficients sum to 6, so the expected weighted average is θ.

B.why: Its expectation is 2θ², not θ².

C.why: Using E(X₃²)=2θ² gives θ+θ².

D.why: Using E(X₂²)=2θ² gives θ−θ².

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Uniform(2θ−1,2θ+1), θ∈R, and let Y₁=min(Xᵢ), Yₙ=max(Xᵢ). Which are maximum likelihood estimators of θ?
options: Statements A, B and C only
items.explanation: The likelihood is constant for values of θ that place every observation inside the interval, and zero otherwise. The support conditions give (Yₙ−1)/2<θ<(Y₁+1)/2. Thus every θ strictly inside this interval is an MLE. The three displayed formulas A, B and C lie inside this interval because Yₙ−Y₁<2 for a sample from a continuous Uniform interval of width 2. Statement D describes the full set of MLEs. All four statements are therefore true.

A.why: The midpoint of the admissible interval lies strictly inside it.

B.why: This weighted combination lies strictly between the support-derived bounds.

C.why: This weighted combination also lies strictly between the support-derived bounds.

D.why: The likelihood is constant and maximal throughout the open admissible interval.

items.stem: A random sample from an exponential distribution with rate λ has sample mean 3.7. Find the MLE of 1−e⁻ˡᵃᵐᵇᵈᵃ, rounded to two decimal places.
items.explanation: For an exponential distribution with rate λ, the MLE is λ̂=1/X̄=1/3.7≈0.27027. By the invariance property of maximum likelihood estimation, the MLE of g(λ)=1−e⁻ˡᵃᵐᵇᵈᵃ is g(λ̂)=1−e⁻¹ᐟ³·⁷≈0.2369, which rounds to 0.24.

items.stem: Let X have density f(x;θ)=θe⁻ᶿˣ for x≥0, θ>0. For testing H₀:θ=1 against H₁:θ>1, reject H₀ when X>log(20). Find the size of the test.
items.explanation: The size is the rejection probability when H₀ is true. Under H₀, X is exponential with rate 1, so P(X>log 20|H₀)=exp(−log 20)=1/20=0.05.
items.check: Under H₀, use the exponential survival function P(X>t)=e⁻ᵗ at t=log 20.

items.stem: Let X~Uniform(θ,θ²), θ>1. Test H₀:θ=2 against H₁:θ=3 by rejecting H₀ when X>3.5. If α is the size and β is the power (as defined in the source), find α+β to two decimal places.
items.explanation: Under H₀, X~Uniform(2,4), so α=P(X>3.5|θ=2)=(4−3.5)/(4−2)=1/4. Under H₁, X~Uniform(3,9), so the power β=P(X>3.5|θ=3)=(9−3.5)/(9−3)=5.5/6=11/12. The source defines β as power, so α+β=1/4+11/12=7/6≈1.17.
items.check: Calculate α=0.25 and power β=11/12; add them to obtain 7/6≈1.17.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,X₁₀ be a random sample from the Laplace location density f(x;θ)=(1/2)e^(−|x−θ|), −∞<x<∞. Which statement about the maximum likelihood estimator of θ is correct?
options: It is not unique in general.
It is always the sample mean.
It is always the smallest observation.
items.explanation: The likelihood is proportional to exp{−Σ|xᵢ−θ|}. Maximising it is equivalent to minimising the sum of absolute deviations from θ. Any sample median minimises this sum. With an even sample size of 10, every value between the fifth and sixth order statistics is a median, so the MLE is generally not unique.

items.stem: A two-sided test of H₀:μ=μ₀ is based on a normal sample with variance assumed to be σ₀², giving p-value p₀. If the actual population variance is smaller, σ₁²<σ₀², what happens to the p-value for the same nonzero observed difference between the sample mean and μ₀ when the correct smaller variance is used?
options: There is no specific relation with p₀.
items.explanation: The two-sided z statistic is |X̄−μ₀|/(σ/√n). For the same observations, replacing σ₀ by the smaller σ₁ makes the denominator smaller and the absolute test statistic larger. A larger absolute z statistic has a smaller two-sided tail probability, so the p-value decreases.

items.stem: Let X₁~Uniform(0,θ) and X₂~Uniform(0,1+θ) independently. Which statistic is sufficient for θ?
items.explanation: The joint density is 1/[θ(1+θ)] when 0<X₁<θ and 0<X₂<1+θ, and zero otherwise. The support restrictions require θ>max(X₁,X₂−1). The likelihood therefore depends on the observations through this maximum only, so the factorisation theorem shows it is sufficient.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a sample from a shifted exponential distribution with unknown location μ and rate λ. Which is a sufficient statistic for (μ,λ)?
items.explanation: The joint density includes the support condition μ≤X₍₁₎ and the factor exp(−λΣXᵢ+nλμ). Write ΣXᵢ=nX₍₁₎+Σ(Xᵢ−X₍₁₎). The likelihood then depends on the observations only through the sample minimum and the sum of deviations from that minimum. This pair is sufficient by factorisation.

items.stem: Let X and Y be iid exponential variables with mean 1/θ, θ>0. For testing H₀:θ=1 against H₁:θ<1, which is the form of the uniformly most powerful test?
options: A UMP test does not exist.
Reject H₀ when X+Y is small.
Reject H₀ when X+Y is large.
items.explanation: For two independent observations, the likelihood ratio for a fixed θ<1 against θ=1 is proportional to exp[(1−θ)(X+Y)]. Since 1−θ>0, it increases with X+Y. The family has a monotone likelihood ratio in the sum, so the UMP test rejects for large values of X+Y.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid N(θ,1), where θ is restricted to integer values. What is the maximum likelihood estimator of θ?
options: The greatest integer less than or equal to X̄.
items.explanation: The normal likelihood is proportional to exp{−(1/2)Σ(Xᵢ−θ)²}. Decompose the sum into Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²+n(X̄−θ)². Maximising the likelihood over integer θ is equivalent to choosing the integer nearest to X̄. If X̄ is exactly halfway between two integers, both maximise the likelihood.

items.stem: For an iid sample from N(μ,σ²), with both μ and σ² unknown, which statements are correct?
statements: S²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/(n−1) is the minimum-variance unbiased estimator of σ².
S=√S² is the minimum-variance unbiased estimator of σ.
Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/n is the maximum likelihood estimator of σ².
√[Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/n] is the maximum likelihood estimator of σ.
items.explanation: For a normal sample, S² with divisor n−1 is unbiased and is the UMVU estimator of σ². The sample standard deviation S is biased for σ, so statement 2 is false. The normal likelihood is maximised at Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/n for σ², and its square root is the MLE of σ. Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true.

A.why: The corrected sample variance is the UMVU estimator of σ².

B.why: The sample standard deviation is biased for σ.

C.why: The normal likelihood gives the divisor-n variance MLE.

D.why: The MLE of σ is the square root of the MLE of σ².

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Uniform(1−θ,1+θ), θ>0. Let X₍₁₎ and X₍ₙ₎ be the sample minimum and maximum, and X̄ the sample mean. Which statements are true?
items.explanation: The likelihood depends on the sample through its minimum and maximum, so including X̄ as well remains sufficient. For Uniform(1−θ,1+θ), E(X)=1 and Var(X)=θ²/3. The expected range is 2θ(n−1)/(n+1), so half the range is biased. Also E[(X−1)²]=θ²/3, making statement 3 unbiased. Finally E[Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²]=(n−1)θ²/3, so statement 4 is biased after scaling by 3/n.

A.why: The sample extrema determine the support restrictions, and the scaled raw squared deviations have the stated expectation.

B.why: The expected half-range is θ(n−1)/(n+1), not θ.

C.why: Each squared deviation from 1 has expectation θ²/3.

D.why: The scaled centred sum has expectation (n−1)θ²/n, not θ².

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Uniform(0,3θ), θ>0, and define Tₙ=(1/3)max(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which statement is NOT true?
statements: Tₙ is a sufficient statistic for θ.
Tₙ is a complete statistic for θ.
items.explanation: The scaled sample maximum is sufficient and complete for the one-parameter uniform scale family. It converges in probability to θ, so it is consistent. Its expectation is nθ/(n+1), which is below θ for every finite n. Therefore it is biased and statement 2 is the one that is not true.

A.why: The sample maximum approaches the upper endpoint 3θ, so Tₙ approaches θ.

B.why: E(Tₙ)=nθ/(n+1), not θ.

C.why: The likelihood depends on θ through the sample maximum.

D.why: The maximum is complete for the uniform scale family.

items.stem: Suppose X₁,…,Xₙ are iid with density f(x|μ,σ)=(1/σ)exp{−(x−μ)/σ}, x>μ, where μ is unknown and σ>0 is known. What is the probability density function of the maximum likelihood estimator of μ?
items.explanation: For this shifted exponential model, the likelihood is largest when μ is as large as possible while remaining below every observation. Therefore the MLE is the sample minimum X₍₁₎. For y>μ, P(X₍₁₎>y)=P(X₁>y,…,Xₙ>y)=[exp{−(y−μ)/σ}]ⁿ=exp{−n(y−μ)/σ}. This is a shifted exponential density with location μ and scale σ/n, so option D is correct.

items.stem: Let X̄ and Ȳ be sample means from two independent samples of sizes m and n from Poisson populations with parameters λ₁ and λ₂, respectively. For large m and n, an asymptotic test of H₀: λ₁=λ₂ against H₁: λ₁≠λ₂ can be based on which statistic?
items.explanation: Under H₀, both sample means estimate the same value λ. By the central limit theorem, X̄ is approximately normal with variance λ₁/m, and Ȳ is approximately normal with variance λ₂/n. Applying the delta method to g(x)=√x gives Var(√X̄)≈1/(4m) and Var(√Ȳ)≈1/(4n) under the null. Thus √X̄−√Ȳ has asymptotic mean zero and a variance that can be estimated without knowing λ. It can be standardised to form the large-sample test statistic, so option C is appropriate.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid N(θ,1), where −100≤θ≤100, and define Yᵢ=0 if Xᵢ<0 and Yᵢ=1 if Xᵢ≥0. Let θ̂ₙ be the MLE based on the full sample and θ̃ₙ the MLE based only on Y₁,…,Yₙ. Which statements are true?
statements: θ̂ₙ is a consistent estimator of θ.
θ̃ₙ is a consistent estimator of θ.
items.explanation: For the full normal sample, the MLE is θ̂ₙ=X̄. It is unbiased because E(X̄)=θ, and its variance is 1/n, so it is consistent. For the sign-only sample, P(Yᵢ=1)=P(Xᵢ≥0)=Φ(θ), where Φ is the standard normal CDF. The sample proportion Ȳ estimates Φ(θ), and the MLE is the inverse transformation Φ⁻¹(Ȳ), constrained to [−100,100] at the endpoints. By the law of large numbers and continuity of Φ⁻¹ at Φ(θ), this estimator is consistent. Since it is bounded in [−100,100], its expectation also converges to θ. Thus all four statements are true.

A.why: The full-sample MLE is X̄ and E(X̄)=θ for every n.

B.why: The sign MLE is bounded and converges in probability to θ, so its expectation also converges to θ.

C.why: Var(X̄)=1/n tends to zero while E(X̄)=θ.

D.why: The sample proportion converges to Φ(θ), and applying the inverse CDF gives θ.

items.repaired: The scan lists four truth statements but no combination choices; standard four-option combinations were supplied. All four statements are true.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be an iid sample from a distribution with density or mass function fθ(x), and let Sₙ²=(1/(n−1))Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)² be the usual sample variance. For which of the following models is Sₙ² an unbiased estimator of θ?
statements: Exponential with mean θ, having density fθ(x)=(1/θ)e^(−x/θ), x>0.
Exponential with rate θ, having density fθ(x)=θe^(−θx), x>0.
items.explanation: For any population with finite variance, the sample variance Sₙ² is unbiased for the population variance. A Poisson(θ) variable has variance θ, so statement A is true. A Normal(0,θ) variable has variance θ, so statement B is also true. An exponential variable with mean θ has variance θ², not θ; statement C is false. An exponential variable with rate θ has variance 1/θ², not θ in general; statement D is false. Therefore A and B only are correct.

A.why: The variance of a Poisson(θ) distribution is θ.

B.why: For Normal(0,θ), the parameter θ is the variance.

C.why: An exponential distribution with mean θ has variance θ².

D.why: An exponential distribution with rate θ has variance 1/θ².

items.repaired: The scan lists four models without combination options; the standard four-option combinations were supplied.

items.stem: A single observation X has a Cauchy distribution with location θ and scale 1, with density fθ(x)=1/[π{1+(x−θ)²}]. For testing H₀:θ=−1 against H₁:θ=0, reject H₀ when X/√(1+X²)>C. What value of C makes the power of the test equal to 0.5?
items.explanation: Power is the probability of rejecting H₀ when H₁ is true. Under H₁, θ=0, so X has a standard Cauchy distribution, which is symmetric about zero. The function g(x)=x/√(1+x²) is strictly increasing and satisfies g(0)=0. Therefore choosing C=0 makes the rejection event exactly X>0. By symmetry, P(X>0)=1/2, so the power is 0.5. Hence option B is correct.

items.stem: A random sample of size n is selected uniformly from the triangular region with vertices (0,0), (0,θ), and (θ,0), where θ>0. Let the observations be (Xᵢ,Yᵢ), i=1,…,n. What is the maximum likelihood estimator of θ?
options: [X₍ₙ₎+Y₍ₙ₎]/2, where X₍ₙ₎=max Xᵢ and Y₍ₙ₎=max Yᵢ
items.explanation: The triangular region has area θ²/2, so the density of one observation is 2/θ² inside the triangle and zero outside. For n independent observations, the likelihood is (2/θ²)ⁿ provided every observation satisfies Xᵢ+Yᵢ≤θ; otherwise it is zero. Thus θ must be at least maxᵢ(Xᵢ+Yᵢ). Within this allowed range, (2/θ²)ⁿ decreases as θ increases, so the likelihood is largest at the smallest allowed value: θ̂=maxᵢ(Xᵢ+Yᵢ).

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from f(x;θ)=θx^(θ−1), 0<x<1, θ>0. The rejection region is {Σᵢ₌₁ⁿlog(Xᵢ)≥c}, where c is suitably chosen. For which testing problems is this a uniformly most powerful region?
items.explanation: The likelihood is proportional to θⁿ exp[(θ−1)Σlog(Xᵢ)]. Therefore the likelihood ratio is increasing in T=Σlog(Xᵢ) when the alternative has larger θ, giving an upper-tail rejection region. This is the UMP form for the one-sided alternative θ>1. It also works for the composite alternative θ≥4 because the least-favourable boundary is θ=4 and the same monotone-likelihood-ratio ordering applies. For alternatives below 4, the appropriate rejection direction is lower-tail; a two-sided alternative does not have this single upper-tail UMP region.

A.why: The family has a monotone likelihood ratio in Σlog(Xᵢ), so the upper-tail region is UMP for θ>1.

B.why: For θ≥4, the boundary θ=4 is least favourable and the same upper-tail region is UMP.

C.why: When θ is below 4, evidence favours smaller values of Σlog(Xᵢ), so the UMP direction is lower-tail.

D.why: A two-sided alternative requires evidence in both directions; a single upper-tail region is not UMP.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Bernoulli(p). Consider testing H₀:p=1/2 against H₁:p=3/4 using the test that rejects H₀ when Σᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ>cₙ, with size α=0.01. Which statement about the limiting power is true?
statements: As n→∞, the power converges to 1/4.
As n→∞, the power converges to 1/2.
As n→∞, the power converges to 3/4.
As n→∞, the power converges to 1.
items.explanation: The critical value cₙ is chosen so that the upper-tail rejection probability under p=1/2 is 0.01. Therefore cₙ is close to n/2 plus a term of order √n. Under the alternative p=3/4, the sum has mean 3n/4 and standard deviation of order √n. The alternative mean exceeds the null critical value by an amount of order n, which is much larger than the standard deviation. Consequently the probability of exceeding cₙ tends to one, so the limiting power is 1.

A.why: The power does not settle at the fixed value 1/4; the alternative mean is far above the critical boundary.

B.why: The alternative distribution moves increasingly far into the rejection region as n grows.

C.why: The limiting rejection probability under p=3/4 is not the parameter value 3/4.

D.why: The critical boundary is near n/2 while the alternative sum is centred at 3n/4, so power tends to one.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Bernoulli(θ), 0<θ<1. Consider T=(Σᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ+√n/2)/(n+√n). As an estimator of θ, which description is correct?
items.explanation: Since E(ΣXᵢ)=nθ, E(T)=(nθ+√n/2)/(n+√n), which is not equal to θ for every θ, so T is biased. To check consistency, divide numerator and denominator by n: T=[X̄+1/(2√n)]/[1+1/√n]. The sample mean X̄ converges in probability to θ, while the added terms tend to zero. Hence T converges in probability to θ and is consistent.

items.stem: A sample of size 7 from N(μ,σ²), with both parameters unknown, gives observations 1.2, 1.3, 1.7, 1.8, 2.1, 2.3 and 2.7. For testing H₀:μ=2 against H₁:μ>2 using the uniformly most powerful one-sided test, what is the decision at both 5% and 1% significance levels?
options: Accept (fail to reject) H₀ at both levels.
Reject at 5% but fail to reject at 1%.
Reject at 1% but fail to reject at 5%.
items.explanation: Because the population is normal and σ² is unknown, the one-sided UMP test uses the one-sample t statistic with 6 degrees of freedom. The sample mean is 1.8714 and the sample standard deviation is about 0.5376, giving t=(1.8714−2)/(0.5376/√7)≈−0.633. The rejection region for H₁:μ>2 is in the upper tail, so this negative statistic is not significant at either 5% or 1%. We therefore fail to reject H₀ at both levels.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,X₁₀₀ be a random sample from N(2,4). Define X̄=(1/99)Σᵢ₌₁⁹⁹Xᵢ, S=√[(1/98)Σᵢ₌₁⁹⁹(Xᵢ−X̄)²], and W=(X₁₀₀−2)/S. What is the distribution of W?
options: Student t with 98 degrees of freedom
Student t with 99 degrees of freedom
items.explanation: The numerator X₁₀₀−2 is independent of the first 99 observations used to calculate S. It has distribution N(0,4), so (X₁₀₀−2)/2 is standard normal. Also, because S² is the sample variance from 99 normal observations, 98S²/4 has a chi-square distribution with 98 degrees of freedom and is independent of the numerator. Therefore W=[Z]/√(χ²₉₈/98), which has a Student t distribution with 98 degrees of freedom.

items.stem: Let X~Uniform(5,5+θ), where θ>0. Based on one observation X₁, which is an unbiased estimator of θ²?
items.explanation: Set Y=X₁−5. Then Y~Uniform(0,θ), whose second moment is E(Y²)=θ²/3. Therefore E[3(X₁−5)²]=3E(Y²)=3(θ²/3)=θ². This proves that option A is unbiased for θ².

items.stem: A random variable has density f(x|θ)=1 for 0<x<1 when θ=0, and f(x|θ)=1/(2√x) for 0<x<1 when θ=1. To test H₀:θ=0 against H₁:θ=1 at level α, 0<α<1, which statements about the most powerful test are true?
statements: The power of the test is √α.
items.explanation: The likelihood ratio is f(x|1)/f(x|0)=1/(2√x), which decreases as x increases. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the most powerful level-α test rejects for small X. Under H₀, X is Uniform(0,1), so choosing the rejection region X<α gives size α. Under H₁, its power is ∫₀ᵅ[1/(2√x)]dx=√α. Thus statements 2 and 4 are true.

A.why: The test rejects for small values of X, not for values larger than 1−α.

B.why: The likelihood ratio decreases in X, so the most powerful rejection region is the lower tail X<α.

C.why: The threshold √α would have null probability √α, not the required size α.

D.why: Integrating the alternative density from 0 to α gives √α.

items.stem: Let X be a continuous random variable. Based on one observation, find the power of the most powerful test of size α=0.1 for testing H₀:f(x)=2x, 0<x<1, against H₁:f(x)=4x³, 0<x<1.
items.explanation: By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, reject H₀ for large values of the likelihood ratio f₁(x)/f₀(x)=2x², so the rejection region is X>c. Under H₀, P(X>c)=∫c¹2x dx=1−c². Setting this equal to 0.1 gives c²=0.9. Under H₁, the power is P(X>c)=∫c¹4x³ dx=1−c⁴=1−(0.9)²=0.19=19/100.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid with density f(x|θ)=2θ²/x³ for x≥θ and zero otherwise, where θ>0 is unknown. What is the maximum likelihood estimator of θ?
items.explanation: The likelihood is L(θ)=(2θ²)ⁿ∏Xᵢ^(−3), provided θ≤Xᵢ for every observation; otherwise it is zero. Thus the allowed parameter values satisfy θ≤min(X₁,…,Xₙ). Within this interval the factor θ^(2n) increases as θ increases. The likelihood is therefore maximised at the largest allowed value, θ̂=min(X₁,…,Xₙ).

items.stem: Let X have density f(x|θ)=2θx+1−θ for 0<x<1, where −1≤θ≤1. Based on one observation, find the most powerful rejection region of size α=0.2 for testing H₀:θ=0 against H₁:θ=1.
items.explanation: Under H₀:θ=0, the density is f₀(x)=1. Under H₁:θ=1, it is f₁(x)=2x. The likelihood ratio f₁(x)/f₀(x)=2x increases with x, so the Neyman–Pearson lemma says to reject H₀ for large values of X. Under H₀, X is Uniform(0,1). To make the test size 0.2, choose c so that P₀(X>c)=0.2, giving c=0.8=4/5.

items.stem: Let (X,Y) have the joint distribution specified by X|Y=y~Binomial(y,0.5) and Y~Poisson(λ), λ>0. Let T=T(X,Y) be any unbiased estimator of λ. Which statements are true?
items.explanation: The marginal variable Y is Poisson(λ), and the conditional distribution of X given Y does not involve λ. Thus Y is sufficient for λ. The Poisson family is complete, so Y is the unique unbiased function of the complete sufficient statistic and is the UMVU estimator of λ. By the Rao–Blackwell and Lehmann–Scheffé results, every unbiased estimator T based on (X,Y) has variance at least Var(Y)=λ. Therefore statements 2 and 3 are true.

A.why: Y is the UMVU estimator, so no unbiased estimator can have smaller variance than Y.

B.why: The Lehmann–Scheffé theorem gives Var(T)≥Var(Y) for every unbiased estimator T.

C.why: Since Var(Y)=λ, the lower bound in statement 2 is exactly λ.

D.why: Equality holds only for estimators that attain the UMVU variance, not for every unbiased estimator.

items.stem: Let X have density f(x|λ)=λ²x e^(−λx), x>0, λ>0. For testing H₀:λ=2 against H₁:λ=1, the most powerful test of size α rejects H₀ when X>c. Which expression gives c?
items.explanation: The likelihood ratio f(x|1)/f(x|2)=(1/4)e^x is increasing in x, so the Neyman–Pearson most powerful test rejects for large X. Under H₀, X has a Gamma distribution with shape 2 and rate 2. Therefore 4X has a chi-square distribution with 4 degrees of freedom. The size condition P₂(X>c)=α is equivalent to P(χ²₄>4c)=α. If χ²₄,α denotes the upper-tail α critical value, then c=(1/4)χ²₄,α.

items.stem: A coin is tossed four times. Let p be the probability of heads in one toss and S the number of heads. Test H₀:p=1/2 against H₁:p≠1/2 by rejecting H₀ when S=0 or S=4. Find the Type I error α and the Type II error β when the true value is p=3/4.
items.explanation: Under H₀, S~Binomial(4,1/2). The rejection probability is P(S=0)+P(S=4)=1/16+1/16=1/8, so α=1/8. When p=3/4, a Type II error occurs when S is 1, 2 or 3. Its probability is 4(3/4)(1/4)³+6(3/4)²(1/4)²+4(3/4)³(1/4)=87/128. Thus the correct pair is α=1/8 and β=87/128.

items.stem: Let X have density f(x|θ)=e^(−(x−θ)) for x>θ and zero otherwise, where θ is unknown. Four observations are 1.7, 1.9, 2.7 and 3.1. Find the maximum likelihood estimate of θ².
items.explanation: For independent observations, the likelihood is exp(−Σxᵢ+4θ) provided θ is smaller than every observation; otherwise it is zero. On the allowed interval θ≤min(xᵢ), this likelihood increases with θ. Hence the MLE is the sample minimum, θ̂=min(1.7,1.9,2.7,3.1)=1.7. By the invariance property of maximum likelihood estimators, the MLE of θ² is θ̂²=1.7²=2.89.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from Uniform(θ−1/2, θ+1/2). Which of the following estimators is not consistent for θ? Use X₍1₎ and X₍n₎ for the minimum and maximum order statistics, respectively.
items.explanation: For a Uniform(θ−1/2,θ+1/2) sample, the minimum X₍1₎ converges in probability to θ−1/2 and the maximum X₍n₎ converges to θ+1/2. Therefore the midrange in option A converges to θ. Options C and D also converge to θ because the first and second smallest order statistics both approach the lower endpoint as n increases. But 1/2+X₍n₎ converges to θ+1, not θ, so it is not consistent.

items.stem: For which of the following distributions is the sample sum ΣXᵢ a sufficient statistic for the unknown parameter?
statements: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Poisson(λ), with λ unknown.
X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Normal(0,σ²), with σ² unknown.
X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Exponential(λ), with rate λ unknown.
X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Bernoulli(p), with p unknown.
items.explanation: For a Poisson sample, the joint likelihood depends on the observations through ΣXᵢ, so the sum is sufficient for λ. For an exponential sample with unknown rate, the likelihood is proportional to λⁿ exp(−λΣXᵢ), so the sum is sufficient. For a Bernoulli sample, the likelihood is proportional to p^(ΣXᵢ)(1−p)^(n−ΣXᵢ), so the sum is sufficient. For a Normal(0,σ²) sample with unknown variance, the likelihood depends on ΣXᵢ², not merely ΣXᵢ; hence the sum is not sufficient.

A.why: The Poisson model has likelihood depending on the sample only through ΣXᵢ.

B.why: For Normal(0,σ²), the sufficient statistic for σ² is ΣXᵢ², not ΣXᵢ.

C.why: The exponential likelihood depends on the data through ΣXᵢ.

D.why: The Bernoulli likelihood depends on the data through the number of successes ΣXᵢ.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,X₅ be iid Poisson(λ), and suppose the observed values are 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. What is the value of the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator (UMVUE) of λ²?
items.explanation: The sum S=ΣXᵢ is a complete sufficient statistic for λ and has a Poisson(5λ) distribution. For a Poisson variable, E[S(S−1)]=(5λ)². Therefore S(S−1)/25 is an unbiased function of the complete sufficient statistic and is the UMVUE of λ². The observed sum is 1+3+5+7+9=25, so the estimate is 25×24/25=24.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid with density fθ(x)=θe^(−θx), x>0, θ>0. Using χ² upper-tail critical-value notation, which of the following are 90% confidence intervals for θ?
items.explanation: For an exponential sample with rate θ, the pivot 2θΣXᵢ has a chi-square distribution with 2n degrees of freedom. With upper-tail notation, χ²₂ₙ,0.95 is the lower 5th percentile and χ²₂ₙ,0.05 is the upper 95th percentile. Inverting the central 90% probability gives the two-sided interval in statement 1. The upper-tail 0.10 critical value gives a one-sided 90% upper confidence bound, producing statement 4. Statement 2 has the wrong one-sided direction for a 90% lower confidence interval, and statement 3 reverses its endpoints.

A.why: The two chi-square quantiles bound the central 90% probability of the pivot.

B.why: With upper-tail notation, this endpoint gives a lower confidence bound with the wrong tail probability for 90% coverage.

C.why: The 0.09 upper-tail quantile is larger than the 0.99 upper-tail quantile, so the interval endpoints are reversed.

D.why: The upper-tail 0.10 critical value yields a one-sided upper confidence bound with 90% coverage.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Exponential with mean θ. What is the UMVUE of 1/θ?
items.explanation: For an exponential distribution with mean θ, the sum S=ΣXᵢ is complete sufficient and has a Gamma distribution with shape n and scale θ. Since E(1/S)=1/[(n−1)θ] for n>1, the estimator (n−1)/S is unbiased for 1/θ. It is a function of the complete sufficient statistic, so it is the UMVUE. Since S=nX̄, this is (n−1)/(nX̄).

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Exponential with mean θ. What is the Cramér–Rao lower bound for the variance of an unbiased estimator of θ²?
items.explanation: For one exponential observation with mean θ, the Fisher information is I₁(θ)=1/θ². For n independent observations, Iₙ(θ)=n/θ². For estimating g(θ)=θ², the derivative is g′(θ)=2θ. The Cramér–Rao lower bound is [g′(θ)]²/Iₙ(θ)=(2θ)²/(n/θ²)=4θ⁴/n.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid with density fθ(x)=3θx²e^(−θx³), x>0, θ>0. What is the maximum likelihood estimator of 1/θ?
items.explanation: The likelihood is L(θ)=3ⁿθⁿ(∏Xᵢ²)exp(−θΣXᵢ³). The log-likelihood, apart from terms not involving θ, is n log θ−θΣXᵢ³. Differentiating and setting equal to zero gives n/θ−ΣXᵢ³=0, so θ̂=n/ΣXᵢ³. By the invariance property of maximum likelihood estimators, the MLE of 1/θ is 1/θ̂=ΣXᵢ³/n.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid with density fθ(x)=x²e^(−x/θ)/(2θ³), x>0, θ>0. What is the maximum likelihood estimator of θ?
items.explanation: The density is that of a Gamma distribution with shape 3 and scale θ. For the sample, the log-likelihood apart from constants is −3n log θ−(ΣXᵢ)/θ. Differentiating gives −3n/θ+(ΣXᵢ)/θ²=0, so θ̂=ΣXᵢ/(3n)=X̄/3. The log-likelihood is maximised at this value.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid from the Laplace density fθ(x)=(1/(2θ))exp(−|x|/θ), θ>0. For testing H₀:θ=θ₀ against H₁:θ=θ₁, where θ₁>θ₀, what is the form of the most powerful test of size α?
options: Reject H₀ when Σ|Xᵢ|<c₁ and Σ|Xᵢ|>c₂.
items.explanation: The likelihood ratio under θ₁ relative to θ₀ is (θ₀/θ₁)ⁿ exp{(1/θ₀−1/θ₁)Σ|Xᵢ|}. Since θ₁>θ₀, the coefficient 1/θ₀−1/θ₁ is positive, so the likelihood ratio increases with Σ|Xᵢ|. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the most powerful test rejects H₀ for sufficiently large values of this sum: Σ|Xᵢ|>c, with c chosen to give size α.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Normal(μ,σ²). Which description of the pair (X̄,S²), where S² is the usual unbiased sample variance, is correct as estimators of (μ,σ²)?
items.explanation: The sample mean satisfies E(X̄)=μ and Var(X̄)=σ²/n, so it is unbiased and its variance tends to zero; hence it is consistent. The usual sample variance S² satisfies E(S²)=σ² and Var(S²)=2σ⁴/(n−1) for a normal sample. Its variance also tends to zero, so it is consistent as well as unbiased. Therefore both estimators are consistent and unbiased.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Normal(μ,σ²), where μ is restricted to the integers. The observed values are 1.7, 2.3, −0.6, −0.8 and 1.5. What is the maximum likelihood estimate of μ?
items.explanation: For a normal sample with known variance, the likelihood as a function of μ is maximised at the sample mean if μ is unrestricted. When μ must be an integer, choose the integer closest to the sample mean. Here X̄=(1.7+2.3−0.6−0.8+1.5)/5=4.1/5=0.82. The closest integer is 1, so the constrained MLE is 1.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid exponential random variables with mean θ. Which of the following is not an unbiased estimator of θ?
items.explanation: For an exponential sample with mean θ, the minimum has expectation E(X₍₁₎)=θ/n, so nX₍₁₎ is unbiased. The sample mean is also unbiased because E(X̄)=θ. The second order statistic has expectation E(X₍₂₎)=θ(1/n+1/(n−1))=θ(2n−1)/[n(n−1)], so multiplying it by (n+1)/2 does not give expectation θ. Finally, E[X₍₁₎+((n−1)/n)X̄]=θ/n+((n−1)/n)θ=θ. Thus option C is not unbiased.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Uniform(0,θ), θ>0. Which of the following statistics are consistent estimators of θ?
statements: (n+1)X₍₁₎, where X₍₁₎ is the sample minimum.
items.explanation: For a Uniform(0,θ) sample, the sample maximum X₍ₙ₎ converges in probability to the upper endpoint θ. Since (n+1)/n tends to 1, the scaled maximum also converges to θ. The sample mean converges to E(X)=θ/2, not θ. The minimum is of order 1/n, and (n+1)X₍₁₎ has a non-degenerate limiting distribution rather than converging to the constant θ. Therefore only statements 1 and 3 are true.

A.why: The sample maximum converges to θ, and multiplying it by (n+1)/n does not change that probability limit.

B.why: The sample mean converges to θ/2, so statement 2 is false.

C.why: The sample mean is inconsistent and the scaled minimum does not converge in probability to θ.

D.why: The sample mean and scaled minimum are not consistent for θ.
